questions.question: What are ActiveRecord migrations and how do you write one?
questions.title: ActiveRecord Migrations Basics
questions.direct_answer: A migration is a Ruby file that changes the database schema in version control — create a table, add a column, add an index. You generate one (rails g migration CreateUsers name:string), which creates a file with a change method; you run rails db:migrate to apply it and rails db:rollback to undo it. Migrations are versioned and run in order, so the schema evolves incrementally and the whole team's databases stay in sync. They let you evolve the schema without writing raw SQL or dropping and recreating tables.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand a migration as a versioned, reversible schema change (change method, db:migrate, db:rollback) that keeps the team's DBs in sync.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Editing a migration that's already been run (others have it; use a new migration instead), or forgetting db:rollback reversibility.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: A migration is a versioned, reversible schema change (create table/add column/index). Generate, db:migrate to apply, db:rollback to undo. Evolve the schema incrementally.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A migration is a versioned, reversible schema change kept in version control.
Generate with rails g migration; the file has a change method (add_column, create_table, add_index).
rails db:migrate applies it; rails db:rollback reverses the last one.
Migrations run in timestamp order, keeping every developer's and prod DB in sync.
Never edit a migration that's been run — write a new one to change the schema further.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A migration is a Ruby file that changes the database schema and is kept in version control — create a table, add a column, add an index. You generate one with rails g migration, which creates a file with a change method describing the change; rails db:migrate applies it to the database, and rails db:rollback undoes the last one. Migrations are versioned with timestamps and run in order, so the schema evolves incrementally and every developer's and the production database stays in sync. They let you evolve the schema without writing raw SQL or dropping and recreating tables, and the change method is reversible — Rails knows how to reverse add_column to remove_column. A key discipline is never to edit a migration that's already been run by others; write a new migration instead, because the old one is already recorded in their database.

sections.title: Migrate and Rollback
sections.content:
db:migrate applies the change; db:rollback reverses it; the schema file records the current state.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[rails g migration] --> F[change method]
  F -->|db:migrate| DB[Database changed]
  F -->|db:rollback| DB2[Database reverted]
  DB --> S[schema.rb snapshot]
```

sections.title: A migration to add a column
sections.content:
```ruby
# Generate: rails g migration AddEmailToUsers email:string
# Creates db/migrate/<ts>_add_email_to_users.rb:

class AddEmailToUsers < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]
  def change
    add_column :users, :email, :string      # reversible: rollback removes it
    add_index :users, :email, unique: true   # add an index too
  end
end

# Apply:   rails db:migrate      # runs the change
# Undo:    rails db:rollback     # reverses the last migration
# Status:  rails db:migrate:status
```
